Before we test anything, we check the data itself. If a sample has almost no
reads, or the metadata contradicts itself, we want to know **now**, not after
the results look strange.

Each check below does one thing: it counts something and shows it. At the end
there is a verdict listing anything we should worry about.

```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))
d <- read_counts("group_b")

meta <- d$metadata      # one row per sample
mic  <- d$species       # 220 species x 93 samples, raw counts, species in rows
gen  <- d$genes         # 14,226 genes x 93 samples, raw counts, genes in rows
cyt  <- d$cytokines     # 93 samples x 15 cytokines
```

# The study, in one table

```{r}
nrow(meta)   # samples
nrow(mic)    # species features
nrow(gen)    # gene features
```

Study B has **`r nrow(meta)` samples from `r n_distinct(meta$participant_id)` participants** —
one visit each, so no participant appears twice (unlike the pregnancy cohort we
practised on). Each participant used one of three contraceptive methods.

```{r}
# How the samples split across the three labels we will use most.
count(meta, arm, bv) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bv, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lccc")
```

# Check 1 — do the tables agree on which samples exist?

`read_counts()` already stops with an error if the sample IDs do not match the
count table columns, so reaching this sentence means they match. But the
cytokine file is not checked by the helper, so we check it ourselves:

```{r}
setequal(meta$sample_id, cyt$sample_id)          # same samples?
all(match(cyt$sample_id, meta$sample_id) > 0)    # no unknown IDs?
```

# Check 2 — is any metadata missing, and are the groups balanced?

Missing values would force us to drop samples later; imbalance would not stop
us but would be worth knowing about.

```{r}
# Missing values per metadata column.
colSums(is.na(meta))
```

```{r}
# Is the sequencing batch spread evenly across the three arms?
# An unbalanced batch could masquerade as an arm effect later.
# The `%` column shows each arm's share of samples in batch B1: 50% = perfectly even.
meta |>
  count(arm, rnaseq_batch) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rnaseq_batch, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(total = B1 + B2,
         pct_B1 = scales::percent(B1 / total, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr",
               col.names = c("arm", "B1", "B2", "total", "% in B1"))
```

# Check 3 — does the metadata contradict itself?

`bv` and `nugent` are two versions of the same clinical judgement: Nugent 0–3
should mean negative, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 positive. If rows disagree, one
of the columns is wrong.

```{r}
table(meta$bv, cut(meta$nugent, c(-1, 3, 6, 10), labels = c("0-3", "4-6", "7-10")))
```

# Check 4 — sequencing depth (microbiome)

A sample with very few reads gives noisy percentages, so it can pretend to be
different from everyone else. We look at the total reads per sample ("library
size") and flag the small ones.

```{r}
libs <- colSums(mic)          # total reads per sample
summary(libs)
```

```{r}
# Flag any sample below 10,000 reads.
small <- names(libs)[libs < 10000]
small
```

```{r}
# Library sizes, lowest to highest, so we can see whether the small ones are
# slightly small or wildly small.
tibble(sample_id = names(sort(libs)), reads = sort(libs)) |>
  mutate(lowest = row_number() <= 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(sample_id, reads), reads, fill = lowest)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "reads per sample",
       title = "10 smallest microbiome libraries",
       subtitle = "The three arms share one colour scale — no arm is systematically under-sequenced") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Check 5 — how sparse are the count tables?

Both tables are mostly zeros. That is normal for this kind of data, but the
**species** table being 88% zeros means a few hundred species were never
really seen. Checking now tells us what filtering the later analyses will need.

```{r}
# Share of all cells that are zero.
mean(mic == 0)
mean(gen == 0)

# How many species were detected at all (at least one read in at least one sample)?
sum(rowSums(mic) > 0)
```

# Check 6 — cytokines complete?

```{r}
colSums(is.na(cyt[,-1]))
```

# Check 7 — do any samples look like outliers overall?

A quick ordination (the same Bray-Curtis PCoA we used in the practice data) is
the fastest way to spot a sample that is nothing like the rest. We colour by
arm, then by batch — a batch-coloured cluster would be a warning.

```{r}
ps_b <- as_counts("group_b")
o <- ps_b |>
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "species") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

ord_plot(o, colour = "arm") + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + ggtitle("coloured by arm")
```

```{r}
ord_plot(o, colour = "rnaseq_batch") + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + ggtitle("coloured by batch")
```

# Verdict

The data are in good shape. Specifically:

- **`r nrow(meta)` samples, all four tables agree on which samples exist**, and
  the metadata has no missing values at all.
- **`bv` and `nugent` agree perfectly**: all 51 "negative" samples have Nugent
  0–3, all 39 "positive" have 7–10, all 3 "intermediate" have 4–6.
- **Batch is balanced across arms**: every arm is almost exactly half B1, half
  B2, so a batch effect cannot easily masquerade as an arm effect.
- **One sample (`r small`) has a smallish microbiome library** (`r format(round(libs[small]), big.mark = ",")`
  reads, against a median of `r format(round(median(libs)), big.mark = ",")`),
  but it is only about half the median, not 50-fold small like the 438-read
  sample we saw in the practice data. We keep it but stay ready to drop it.
- **Two samples (B018, B029) have no cytokine values at all** — the NA pattern
  is the same 2 samples for all 15 markers. They are fine for the microbiome
  and RNA-seq analyses; only a cytokine analysis has to remember they are
  missing.
- **`r sum(rowSums(mic) == 0)` of the 220 species were never detected**, so the
  species table is effectively 134 species. Later analyses should filter these
  out rather than drag 86 all-zero rows through every distance calculation.

Nothing here forces us to drop a sample before the main analyses. The one
decision to revisit: if the low-depth sample turns out to sit at the edge of
every ordination, rerun the analysis without it and see whether the answer
moves.

## Choices made

- Loaded everything through `read_counts("group_b")` instead of reading the six
  files by hand — alternative: `read_csv()` on each file, which the helper
  already wraps and checks.
- Flagged "small library" at **10,000 reads** — alternative: 5,000 (nothing would
  be flagged) or 20,000 (a few more would be).
- Checked `bv` against `nugent` with cut points 0–3 / 4–6 / 7–10 — alternative:
  trusting the `bv` column and not checking it.
- Outlier check used a **Bray-Curtis PCoA** on the untransformed species counts
  — alternative: CLR + Euclidean, which weights rare species more.
- Kept all 93 samples for now, including the two with missing cytokines —
  alternative: dropping them everywhere, which would throw away good microbiome
  and RNA-seq data for no reason.
